title: Antikythera mechanism
wiki_lead:
The Antikythera mechanism ( AN-tik-ih-THEER-ə, US also  AN-ty-kih-) is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery (model of the Solar System) built in the 2nd century BC and discovered in 1901. It is the oldest known example of an analogue computer. It could be used to predict astronomical positions and eclipses decades in advance. It could also be used to track the four-year cycle of athletic games similar to an olympiad, the cycle of the ancient Olympic Games.
The artefact was among wreckage retrieved from a shipwreck off the coast of the Greek island Antikythera in 1901. In 1902, during a visit to the National Archaeological Museum in Athens, it was noticed by Greek politician Spyridon Stais as containing a gear, prompting the first study of the fragment by his cousin, Valerios Stais, the museum director. The device, housed in the remains of a wooden-framed case of (uncertain) overall size 34 cm × 18 cm × 9 cm (13.4 in × 7.1 in × 3.5 in), was found as one lump, later separated into three main fragments which are now divided into 82 separate fragments after conservation efforts. Four of these fragments contain gears, while inscriptions are found on many others. The largest gear is about 13 cm (5 in) in diameter and originally had 223 teeth. All these fragments of the mechanism are kept at the National Archaeological Museum, along with reconstructions and replicas, to demonstrate how it may have looked and worked.
In 2005, a team from Cardiff University led by Mike Edmunds used computer X-ray tomography and high resolution scanning to image inside fragments of the crust-encased mechanism and read faint inscriptions that once covered the outer casing. These scans suggest that the mechanism had 35 meshing bronze gears, 30 of which are still visible, enabling it to follow the movements of the Moon and the Sun through the zodiac, to predict eclipses and to model the irregular orbit of the Moon, where the Moon's speed is higher in its perigee than in its apogee. This motion was studied in the 2nd century BC by astronomer Hipparchus of Rhodes, and he may have been consulted in the machine's construction. There is speculation that a portion of the mechanism is missing and it calculated the positions of the five classical planets. The inscriptions were further deciphered in 2016, revealing numbers connected with the synodic cycles of Venus and Saturn.
The instrument is believed to have been designed and constructed by Hellenistic scientists and been variously dated to about 87 BC, between 150 and 100 BC, or 205 BC. It must have been constructed before the shipwreck, which has been dated by multiple lines of evidence to approximately 70–60 BC. In 2022, researchers proposed its initial calibration date, not construction date, could have been 23 December 178 BC. Other experts propose 204 BC as a more likely calibration date. Machines with similar complexity did not appear again until the 14th century in western Europe.

grok_lead: The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand-powered orrery, recognized as the world's oldest known analog computer and often popularly referred to as the "first computer in the world", constructed around the late 2nd century BC from at least 30 meshing bronze gears housed within a shoebox-sized wooden case. Discovered in 1901 amid the wreckage of a Roman cargo ship off the Greek island of Antikythera, the device survives in 82 corroded fragments and was originally housed in a wooden case measuring about 340 mm Ã 180 mm Ã 90 mm; it is now preserved in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. It functioned as a mechanical calculator for predicting celestial phenomena, including the positions of the Sun, Moon, and likely the five known planets (Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn) along the zodiac, as well as lunar and solar eclipses. At its core, the mechanism integrated advanced astronomical models of the era, such as Hipparchus's theory of lunar anomaly using epicyclic gearing to simulate irregular motions, alongside Babylonian arithmetic cycles for eclipse forecasting via the 223-month Saros dial. The front face featured two concentric dials: a large one displaying the lunar calendar date (a ring with 354 or 355 holes tracking the Greek lunar year, as confirmed by 2024 statistical modeling techniques adapted from gravitational wave analysis that also demonstrated high-precision hole placement with 0.028 mm average radial variation) and zodiac positions, with pointers for the Sun and Moon (with a small rotating half-black half-white sphere on the Moon pointer indicating the lunar phases), while the rear included spiral dials for the 19-year Metonic lunisolar cycleâmarking Corinthian months and intercalary adjustmentsâand a Games dial listing the four Panhellenic games and indicating the position within the four-year Olympiad cycle. Inscriptions in ancient Greek, now doubled in deciphered volume through modern imaging like X-ray computed tomography, provided operational instructions, planetary period relations (e.g., 462 synodic periods for Venus and 442 for Saturn), and mythological references, revealing its Corinthian origins and ties to Greek cosmology with Earth at the center. This device's sophistication, involving precise gear ratios (up to 1:127 for differential turns) and triangular teeth, far exceeded any surviving machinery until the European clockwork of the 14th century AD, highlighting a pinnacle of Hellenistic engineering that integrated mathematics, astronomy, and craftsmanship. Its loss in the shipwreck approximately 70â60 BC underscores a technological discontinuity, as no comparable geared mechanisms appear in records until much later, prompting ongoing research into its design influences from astronomers like Hipparchus and its potential educational or navigational uses. Modern reconstructions, informed by polynomial texture mapping and 3D modeling, confirm its predictive accuracy for astronomical positions and eclipses decades in advance; however, a 2025 simulation study found that manufacturing inaccuracies measured from CT scans (including those analyzed by Edmunds) would likely have caused gears to jam or disengage after limited operation, with gear spacing contributing to the risk in simulationsâthe authors conclude that either the mechanism never functioned properly or the measured errors were overestimated due to possible issues with CT scan accuracy or corrosion effects, while considering a deliberately non-functional construction unlikely., cementing its status as a "lost" marvel of antiquity.
